title: Security review: encryption, KMS/BYOK/HSM
summary: Redwood (AE+SE) walked Acme Health security and cloud engineering through encryption options: default managed KMS, BYOK import, Cloud HSM integrations, key rotation, and audit logging. Discussed residency requirements and Private deployment implications. Action items captured: send KMS architecture doc, SOC 2 report, schedule SE deep dive for HSM integration and benchmark for dedicated/private deployment.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-11-25 16:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Acme Health Security Lead), Lina Chen (Acme Health Cloud Eng), Oliver Hayes (CISO)

[00:00] Alex: All right, hi everyone, thanks for carving out time. This is Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, and Priya our solutions engineer is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Marcus: Hey Alex, thanks. Doing well. We just want to run through our encryption and key management concerns before we move forward.
[00:12] Alex: Totally. We're planning to cover encryption in transit and at rest, KMS options including BYOK, HSM support, key rotation and compromise procedures, audit logging and retention, and then any residency or private deployment implications. Sound good?
[00:22] Lina: Yep, that's perfect. Our main constraints are: keys must be customer-owned for PHI flows, audit logs need to be retained for 7 years, and we need SSO with SCIM and SAML -- and RBAC rules enforced.
[00:33] Priya: Great, thanks for the context. Quick note: some folks use Redwood Hosted with customer-managed keys, and others run Redwood Private in their VPCs; we'll outline tradeoffs.
[00:41] Oliver: I'm mainly interested in the HSM question — does Redwood integrate with our cloud HSM or on-prem HSM?
[00:47] Priya: Short answer: yes, we support both cloud HSM integrations (we've done AWS CloudHSM and Google Cloud HSM projects) and we support BYOK imports for customers who prefer to manage keys in their KMS. For fully air-gapped on-prem HSMs, that's typically part of a Redwood Private engagement; we'll want a technical deep dive to scope network connectivity and the key wrapping flow.
[01:02] Marcus: When you say BYOK import, do you mean we upload a key material blob into Redwood's KMS, or you wrap keys with our KMS? We can't have plaintext key material leave our control.
[01:12] Priya: Good question. We support multiple patterns: 1) Envelope encryption where customer KMS (e.g., AWS KMS) wraps a data key and we never see plaintext key material — we hold the wrapped key; 2) External key references where the crypto operations are proxied to your KMS via APIs; and 3) For Private deployments we can integrate directly with your HSM using PKCS#11 or cloud HSM APIs so keys never leave your HSM. We do not require customers to hand us unencrypted master keys.
[01:36] Lina: That envelope flow sounds closest to our requirement. Can you explain how rotation and re-encryption work? We have a long retention period and need to be able to rotate keys without downtime.
[01:46] Priya: Sure. Our recommended model is envelope encryption: we generate short-lived data keys for encrypting model caches, token indices, and storage objects; those data keys are themselves encrypted (wrapped) by a customer-managed master key. Rotation is a key policy change: you can rotate the master wrap key in the KMS, and we re-wrap existing data keys lazily on first use or proactively via a rewrap job. For massive datasets we offer a rewrap job that can stream and rewrap objects with batching to avoid latency spikes. For runtime caches we do lazy rewrap to avoid blocking requests.
[02:15] Marcus: Is the rewrap job auditable? We need immutable logs showing when a key was rotated and by whom.
[02:21] Priya: Yes — all key wrap/unwrapping operations are logged. On Hosted we surface audit logs through the Redwood Console with immutable append-only records, and you can export to your SIEM via syslog/S3 hooks. For Private deployments you control where logs are shipped. We also support log signing so the log entries are tamper-evident.
[02:40] Oliver: What's the retention/availability SLAs on those logs if we're on Redwood Hosted? We need seven years on different legal holds.
[02:47] Alex: By default we retain operational audit logs for 1 year in the hosted tier, but for enterprise customers we offer configurable retention packages and archival to your own object storage for long-term retention. We'll include archival S3 export and export lifecycle policies in the contract.
[03:02] Lina: Okay, good. A couple of security specifics: FIPS compliance and HSM certification. We run in a regulated environment — FIPS 140-2 / 140-3 validated HSMs are required in our environment.
[03:13] Priya: We commonly integrate with FIPS-validated cloud HSMs (AWS CloudHSM, Google Cloud HSM) or customer-provided FIPS HSMs. Redwood's software stack doesn't require FIPS validation itself when keys are managed in a FIPS HSM and crypto ops happen there. If you need full supply chain FIPS attestation that's something we'll scope in Professional Services.
[03:31] Marcus: What about key compromise procedures? If a master key is compromised, how do we handle rekey and data protection?
[03:38] Priya: Standard approach: rotate the master key immediately, issue a new wrap key, and re-wrap data keys. For emergency we can also rotate by generating a new data key under a new master and update live caches. We have documented playbooks with runbooks, steps for secret rotation, and we can integrate with your incident response to automate parts of it. We'll also provide an audit trail for every step.
[03:57] Alex: Can I add — Redwood has a capability to fall back to a secondary key store for emergency reads if the primary KMS is unavailable, but that requires configuration and contractual acceptance since it has security implications. Most customers prefer to accept temporary unavailability over fallback keys.
[04:12] Oliver: We prefer no automatic fallback. We want explicit failover with approvals.
[04:17] Priya: Noted. We can configure manual failover and maintain a strict approval workflow in the Console.
[04:23] [05:00] Marcus: How about encryption at rest on disk vs object storage? Does Redwood encrypt ephemeral caches, model artifacts, and embeddings store?
[05:10] Priya: Yes — everything at rest is encrypted. For Hosted we use provider-managed storage that is encrypted and we layer envelope encryption for customer datasets and artifacts. For Dedicated and Private, you can provide your own encrypted object storage and we can use your KMS to wrap keys. Ephemeral GPU / local disk caches are encrypted as well.
[05:28] Lina: Does traffic between the compute plane and storage plane use mutual TLS? We have concerns about lateral movement inside cloud regions.
[05:35] Priya: All internal traffic is TLS 1.2+ and we support mTLS for Private deployments and Dedicated clusters. For Hosted we enforce strict TLS and internal network segmentation; for Private you'll get mutual TLS and can restrict networks with VPC peering and security groups.
[05:50] Alex: Also worth noting: requests between the control plane and data plane are authenticated with short-lived tokens; we avoid long-lived credentials on the compute nodes.
[05:58] Marcus: Can we rotate those tokens frequently?
[06:01] Priya: Yes, token lifetimes are configurable, and we support automatic rotation and revocation via the Console or APIs.
[06:07] [06:30] Oliver: Auditability: can we get a proof-of-where-keys-live statement to present to auditors? Like a chain-of-custody doc?
[06:38] Alex: Yes, we have a Key Custody & Crypto Architecture doc that lays out key locations, who has custody, and integration patterns. We'll share that doc and our SOC 2 type II report.
[06:48] Marcus: Please also include the HSM attestation docs if you integrated with cloud HSMs.
[06:52] Priya: We'll include HSM vendor attestations and the architectural diagram showing PKCS#11 or Cloud KMS APIs.
[06:59] [07:15] Lina: One more question about data residency. Some of our data must remain in Canada and EU. Does Redwood let us pin region for key storage and artifact storage?
[07:25] Priya: Yes, we can pin key residency and object residency. For Hosted customers we have regional clusters and can pin your project to a region; for Dedicated you get region-specific capacity and for Private you're hosting in your region entirely. The BYOK envelope model keeps keys in your KMS region when you want.
[07:42] Marcus: Are there any limitations on model variants or performance implications when using BYOK vs Redwood-managed keys?
[07:49] Priya: Minimal performance impact when using envelope encryption; however, if you proxy crypto calls to a remote KMS for every operation, that adds latency. Our recommended pattern is to cache wrapped data keys locally for short TTLs so crypto calls to the KMS are amortized. We can show benchmarks — there is a small tail latency increase if KMS calls are in the critical path.
[08:09] Alex: That's where Redwood Dedicated helps — lower network latency to your KMS and the ability to colocate in the same cloud region or VPC.
[08:16] Marcus: Let's talk about logs again — we need tamper-evident audit logs for KMS ops, and separation of duties so only a handful of people can trigger rewraps.
[08:26] Priya: Console RBAC supports role-based controls; we integrate with SSO (SAML/Okta) and SCIM for provisioning. Audit events are available and can be exported to your SIEM. For separation of duties, we can support multi-approver workflows for key operations in the enterprise Console.
[08:41] Lina: Do you support hardware-backed keys on customer side with CloudHSM and hold private keys there while Redwood only gets wrapped keys?
[08:49] Priya: Yes, that's the typical pattern: keep the master key in CloudHSM, use KMS to wrap/unwrap data keys, Redwood never sees plaintext master keys. For Private we can also hook to your on-prem PKCS#11 HSM.
[09:00] Oliver: In terms of compliance evidence, we'll need logs of key creation, rotation, deletion, and who approved them, plus any KMS API call traces.
[09:08] Priya: We produce those events; for Hosted we can stream raw events to your SIEM or S3. For Dedicated/Private you can retain full control over logs and the retention policy.
[09:19] [09:40] Marcus: What about rate limits — does Redwood provider KMS proxy limit API calls to our KMS and could we hit throttling that affects production?
[09:47] Priya: We have a KMS call-throttling and backoff layer. If your KMS is throttling we queue and exponential-backoff, and we also provide guidance on batch sizes and TTLs for data keys to avoid high QPS. For high-throughput workloads we recommend caching and periodic refresh rather than per-request KMS calls. We'll include guidance in the architecture doc.
[10:08] Alex: Quick note on termination and key destruction: if you terminate service, you retain your keys in your KMS; we can provide a zero-knowledge wipe of local wrapped keys and deliver a proof of deletion. We'll coordinate the export of any logs/artifacts per contract.
[10:24] Lina: Good. For eDiscovery / legal holds — if we need to put a hold on certain data, can Redwood freeze deletion and preserve data while retaining encryption config?
[10:34] Priya: Yes, we support legal hold policies at the object level and can prevent lifecycle deletion. The retention policies are configurable and can be enforced on Dedicated/Private deployments as well.
[10:44] Marcus: On SOC 2 and ISO, do you have both reports? We need evidence for our GRC team.
[10:50] Alex: We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certifications. We'll share redacted reports and the relevant control mappings to demonstrate how KMS, encryption, and access controls map to requirements.
[10:59] [11:15] Oliver: Any known gaps or workarounds we should be aware of?
[11:19] Priya: A few practical notes: 1) Using customer-managed KMS without caching can raise latency; 2) If you require air-gapped HSMs you should expect professional services and longer onboarding; 3) Some third-party model variants may require model weights stored in object storage — we'll need to verify residency requirements for those.
[11:39] Lina: Understood. We also want to run an integration test where we simulate KMS outage and observe behavior.
[11:45] Priya: We can do that in a staged POC. We can simulate KMS latency, turn off KMS access, and validate failover behavior in a dedicated environment.
[11:55] Marcus: Good. Let's record a few next steps and owners.
[12:00] Alex: Sure - recap: we'll send KMS architecture doc, SOC2 and ISO artifacts, HSM attestation docs, and a proposed configuration for key rotation and retention. Priya will schedule a technical deep dive with your infra team for HSM and PKCS#11 integration and we'll scope a POC that includes a simulated KMS outage.
[12:18] Oliver: Also send over the Console RBAC screenshots and multi-approver workflow details.
[12:24] Priya: Will do. Anything else?
[12:28] Marcus: One last item — pricing for the retention add-on for 7-year archival.
[12:32] Alex: We'll include that in the follow-up email and attach the contract appendix.
[12:36] [12:40] Meeting end notes: general agreement on architecture; need to schedule SE deep dive and POC. Quality of transcript medium, some names may be slightly off in auto-transcription.
